Emigration

/em-ih-GRAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Emigration means the act of leaving your own country in order to settle permanently in another

In the 1950s, years of job shortages in southern Italy drove a wave of emigration to Argentina and Canada.

Worked Example

The physics institute struggled after years of emigration thinned its research staff, as one scientist after another accepted permanent positions abroad.

The scientists are not just changing jobs — they are leaving the country to settle abroad, so their departure counts as emigration (a pattern sometimes called a brain drain).

How Emigration Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

exodus

exodus: a mass departure of people from a place

expatriation

expatriation: leaving one's homeland to live elsewhere

relocation

relocation: moving to live in a new place

Antonyms

repatriation

repatriation: returning to live in one's home country

homecoming

homecoming: a return to one's home

How Strong Is It? — relocation → emigration → exodus

relocation vs. emigration

relocation vs. emigration: Relocation is milder than emigration: a family can relocate across town without leaving behind anything but an address.

exodus vs. emigration

exodus vs. emigration: Exodus is stronger than emigration: it suggests a whole population streaming out at once, like an entire region emptying within a single generation.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out of (a form of ex-)

Root — migr

Root — migr: to move from one place to another (Latin migrare)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin emigrare: e- (out) + migrare (to move) + -ation (act of) — the act of moving out of one's homeland.

Use the root in a new word: immigrant

Use the root in a new word: immigrant: Her grandfather arrived as an immigrant in 1962, carrying one suitcase and his mother's recipes.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / academic

Emigration looks at the journey from the country being left: you emigrate FROM a place. Immigration is the very same journey seen from the destination: you immigrate TO a place. A Polish family's emigration from Poland is, to Canadians, immigration to Canada — one move, two vantage points. The e- (out) and im- (in) prefixes tell you which direction the word is facing.
